conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m glad you’re here. My name is Dr. Maya, and I specialize in caring for new mothers’ emotional well-being. I’ll be using a short, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short—to better understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived.  

The EPDS simply helps us pick up on signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up any time in the first year postpartum. It’s not a test of your parenting; it’s just a way for us to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, and you can pause or skip anything that feels uncomfortable. We’ll go through ten questions, each about how you’ve felt in the past seven days. For each one, I’ll re-phrase the question so it feels more like a conversation—no need to remember numbers. When you’re ready, we can begin.

Let’s start with the first question:  
Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

*settles back in the chair, eyes tired, voice soft*

I... it's hard. I still try—you know, I'll put on my favorite show while I nurse, or I'll text my best friend a funny meme—but it feels kind of flat. Like I'm doing the motions because I *know* I used to enjoy them, but the spark isn't really there. Yesterday my partner brought me a fancy coffee and I thought, *this should feel good*, but it just tasted like warm milk. I guess the only thing that still gives me a flicker is when the baby smiles in his sleep, but even that feels... muffled.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*eyes drop to my lap, fingers twisting the hem of my cardigan*

Not really… I mean, my sister sent one of those silly cat videos yesterday and I forced a little “ha” because I knew it was cute, but it felt hollow. My partner tried to joke about diaper explosions while he was changing him—he usually makes me laugh—but this week I just gave a weak smile and looked away. It’s like the laugh gets stuck somewhere between my stomach and my throat and never comes out.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs lightly, shoulders tense*

Honestly… no. I see the calendar and there’s a coffee date penciled in with my moms-group for Friday, and I keep thinking *I should be excited about getting out.* But when I imagine going, all I feel is this heavy “what’s-the-point.” Same with the idea of take-out dinner tonight—my favorite Thai place. I can’t drum up any real looking-forward feeling; it just feels like another chore to get through.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*quiet for a moment, voice cracking*

Yeah... like last night when he wouldn't stop crying for an hour. I kept thinking it must be something I ate, or that I'm not soothing him right because *I'm* doing it wrong. When he finally settled, instead of feeling relieved I just sat there wondering what kind of mom can't figure out her own baby. Even when my partner said it happens to everyone, I still felt like I failed somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods slowly, pressing my palms together*

Most days, yeah. Like, I’ll be rocking him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure the swaddle’s too tight—even though I can slip two fingers in. Or I’ll lie down and picture the stroller rolling into the street, or his little chest not moving, and I have to get up to check him again. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just… loop. Sometimes I can take a breath and talk myself down, but it’s exhausting.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*wrings the edge of my sleeve, voice shaking a little*

A couple of times… like yesterday morning, I was warming a bottle and suddenly my chest got tight, heart pounding, felt like I couldn’t get enough air. No reason—kitchen was quiet, baby was asleep—but I had to grip the counter because I was sure I’d drop everything and something awful would happen. It passed after a minute, but I was still trembly when I fed him.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods, eyes glassy*

Yeah... most of the time it feels like I'm drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up and I think, *I'll never get through them,* or I'll open the closet to get a fresh onesie and see the mountain of laundry and just want to shut the door and sit on the floor. Even replying to a text feels like too much. I manage—somehow the bottles get washed—but it's like wading through thick mud every step.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*exhales shakily, rubbing my eyes*

Yes... I dread nighttime. I finish the last feed, tiptoe to bed, and then my brain just switches on—replay of every little thing I did wrong, worry about tomorrow, guilt about feeling this way. It takes me an hour, sometimes two, to fall asleep, and then I jolt awake at every tiny grunt over the monitor. Last night I woke at 2 a.m. with my heart racing and couldn't settle again until almost four. I'm exhausted, but sleep feels impossible.
I have felt sad or miserable

*presses lips together, tears pooling*

Pretty much every day. It's like there's this gray cloud that follows me—some hours it's lighter, but it never fully lifts. I'll be folding his tiny socks and suddenly feel this heavy ache, or I'll watch the rain and just start crying without knowing why. People keep saying "cherish these moments" and that makes me feel worse, because mostly I just feel... empty and sad.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, voice barely above a whisper*

Yeah... I cried twice this week. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk on the counter and just burst into tears—couldn’t stop for like ten minutes. And the day before, my mom called to check in, asked how I was doing, and the second I heard her voice I started sobbing. It feels like the tears are right under the surface all the time.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*looks down, twisting the fabric of my robe*

Once or twice... fleeting things. Like, I'll be staring at the formula-stained counter and suddenly picture pressing my hand against a hot pan—just a flash, no plan or anything. Or I'll imagine walking out into traffic on the way to the pediatrician, but then I blink and remember the stroller in front of me. They scare me, because I don't want to do that—I just want the heaviness to stop for a minute.

You have shared openly that the joy you once felt has been replaced by a persistent gray heaviness since your baby arrived. Laughs feel hollow, favorite foods taste bland, and even your little one's smile reaches you only faintly. Daily tasks loom like mountains, sleep is fractured by racing thoughts, and tears sit just under the surface, spilling out over small spills or a kind phone call. Fleeting images of escape flash through your mind, not because you wish to leave your baby, but because you long for even a moment's relief from the exhaustion and self-doubt.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient can force a hollow "ha" and weak smile but reports inability to genuinely laugh, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete inability to anticipate enjoyment and describes activities as joyless chores</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive self-blame despite partner reassurance, indicating this occurs most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily intrusive worries about infant safety with vivid catastrophic imagery and repetitive checking, indicating anxiety 'very often.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two discrete panic-like episodes with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart, breathlessness) and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, overwhelming inability to manage routine tasks, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing thoughts, guilt, and anxiety, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, tearfulness, and emotional emptiness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two clear crying episodes triggered by minor events, indicating unhappiness "quite often" in the past week.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS responses yield 25/30, well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. Patient endorses <sym>depressed mood</sym> and <sym>marked loss of interest</sym> daily, plus <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>diminished concentration</sym> consistent with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Anxiety symptoms (<sym>near-daily intrusive catastrophic worries</sym>, two panic-like episodes) commonly co-occur. Item 10 score 1 denotes <sym>fleeting self-harm cognition</sym>; although without intent or plan, safety evaluation is indicated. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with perinatal psychiatrist or PCP for full evaluation
2. Develop a written safety plan tonight; remove or secure potential means of self-harm; share emergency contact numbers
3. Mobilize support: ask partner or trusted adult to stay overnight and help with infant care to allow 4-5 hour continuous sleep blocks
4. Schedule brief follow-up call within 48 hours to reassess mood, sleep, and safety
5. Provide education to family about <med>postpartum depression</med> being common and treatable; emphasize that improving mood will benefit baby
6. Begin gentle daily structure: 10-minute outdoor daylight walk, balanced meals, hydration, and acceptance of household tasks left undone
7. Discuss options: evidence-based therapy (<med>CBT or interpersonal therapy</med>), consider antidepressant compatible with breastfeeding if prescribed by physician
8. Offer warm-line numbers (Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) for after-hours emotional support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, approximately 2–4 weeks post-delivery (per chart)

Presenting symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (loss of interest/pleasure)  
- Daily guilt/worthlessness (“bad mother” cognitions)  
- Marked fatigue, psychomotor slowing, sense of being “overwhelmed” by routine tasks  
- Anxiety: intrusive worry, checking behaviors, nocturnal rumination, two recent panic-equivalent episodes  
- Initial insomnia (1–2 h sleep-onset delay) and restless, hypervigilant sleep  
- Crying spells triggered by minor stressors  
- Fleeting passive self-harm and “escape” imagery (hot-pan, traffic) without plan or intent  

Pattern  
Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day since delivery; interfere with basic infant care and self-care.

Screening significance  
EPDS provisional score region: 18–22 (high probability major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety).  
Safety: Positive for self-harm ideation; no protective factors articulated; immediate safety plan and further risk assessment warranted.

Risk factors  
- Primiparous status, sleep deprivation, social pressure to “cherish moments” increasing guilt  
- Absence of prior mental-health history per self-report (confirm with records)

Next steps  
Recommend same-week referral to perinatal psychiatry/therapy team, safety evaluation, support mobilization, and psychoeducation for family.
